This paper presents a generalization of an existing statistical model, the TEXPAR, by incorporating time-varying coefficients into the classic PAR framework to create the TEVAR model. While both models share the same underlying structure of an AR(1) model, we found through comparison that the TEVAR model better captures the dynamics of real-world data sets due to its unrestricted time-dependent coefficients, as opposed to the constant beta values in the TEXPAR model. Moreover, we developed a sophisticated estimation method combining nonlinear least squares and iterative procedures to estimate the TEVAR model's matrix of coefficients, which can be represented as a function of time using polynomial approximation.

While using photometry to monitor air quality is not a new concept, our paper is what makes it possible to effectively do so on a broad scale by employing wide field stellar photometry.  Data obtained from the HAT-NET project, which tracks transiting exoplanets, was analyzed to determine its suitability for determining aerosol optical depth (AOD).  Using NASA's MODIS satellite data as a reference, we analyzed data from ten telescopes across North America and a carousel telescope in Australia.  After conducting linear regression analysis on data with a CRI greater than 0.9, we found that there was a strong correlation between photometric data and AOD, with correlation coefficients of 0.73 for North American telescopes and 0.70 for the Australian telescope.  We also observed a seasonal variation in AOD readings, likely caused by changes in weather patterns, and found that the average AOD was lower when observations were conducted during the day as opposed to at night.  While using wide field photometry to monitor aerosols is limited in precision when comparing it to lidar or radar technology, we believe this is the first time that doing so has been possible with a large network of small telescopes.  This method could be particularly beneficial in areas that lack extensive air quality monitoring infrastructure.

Our research presents an improved iterative algorithm for solving the Schrödinger equation, which serves as the foundation for a quantum-informed molecular dynamics method. By incorporating the electron density calculated from the iterative solution into the Langevin force, we achieve more efficient and accurate molecular sampling, especially for strongly bonded molecules, as opposed to classical force fields. Our optimized algorithm reduces computational time and expands the range of molecules applicable, demonstrated through testing on water and methanol molecules, showing significant improvements in sampling efficiency measured by acceptance rates and discrete time step sizes.

Human-centric evaluation metrics are widely used in image description evaluation, raising the question of whether current standards are representative. A study found that ranking methods, including those used in competitions, may not be as effective as anticipated. A new metric, K-Shortlist Accuracy, was developed to better assess performance, revealing that models considered state-of-the-art do not outperform random selection when evaluating 100 descriptions. The paper concludes that validation sets used in competitions are not sufficiently diverse and advocates for more representative data, potentially impacting how models are evaluated and selected.

We integrate intricate aspects of conformal field theory (CFT) complexity with recently developed equations known as conformal Euler-Arnold equations. Specifically, we demonstrate that the third-order differential equation governing the primary operator generating function in free fermion 2d CFT models is equivalent to the first-order model. Moreover, we demonstrate that the highest-order correction in the theory's scaling dimension deviation from a critical value of zero in freely generated functions corresponds to the incompressibility condition in fluid dynamics. Consequently, we are able to identify a compressible, inhomogeneous example using an inhomogeneous cubic term.
Based on the lambda CDM model, we propose two minor extensions: a constant distribution of dark baryons and a specific meson spectrum remaining in the universe.
This article presents variations of an innovative waveforming technique introduced previously.

Integrating experimental data with theoretical predictions to infer physical parameters is a challenging task that involves dealing with disparate data types and theoretical calculations. This difficult process, known as paper fitting, is addressed by a comprehensive framework developed specifically for parton distribution function (PDF) fitting. This framework, which is modular and object-oriented, features a sophisticated data handling system capable of processing various experimental inputs while also incorporating a robust statistical inference engine. What makes this framework unique is its modular design, which is highly customizable and extensible, enabling a flexible and adaptable PDF fitting procedure. Furthermore, this framework is documented in both code and API formats to facilitate its use by researchers.

This study uses linearized equations to investigate the response of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic vibrations, with a focus on flame shape fluctuations. Unlike previous studies that focus on smoke ring instability, our research aims to analyze the causes of flame shape instability in an active flame model, taking into account fluid dynamics effects such as convection and the reaction dynamics of chemistry. To better understand the role of these factors, we developed a model that allows us to adjust the response of the flame to vibrations. By performing simulations with varying timescales of chemical reactions in a passive scalar model, we found that the shape of the spectrum curve is affected, with a peak shifting to lower frequencies as the reaction becomes more rapid. Additionally, we discovered that the overall amplitude of the response decreases as the reaction becomes faster, resulting in broader peaks for longer chemistry timescales. To further analyze the results, we conducted a fit to the spectrum using a two-degree-of-freedom approach, which allowed us to identify the influence of various forces, including body and pressure forces as well as source terms related to chemistry. Our research found that the response of the flame to vibrations is primarily driven by the coupling between the flame shape and acoustic waves, with the source term playing a secondary role in amplifying the vibration.

Momentum constitutive equations in general tensor theory involve complex multi-index notations, simplifying them to use only single-index representations. Within the framework of S. Weibel's nonlocal gravity, we define fundamental frames for both Minkowski and curved spaces, and explicitly define speed and light cones for use in nonlocal operators.

The upcoming high-energy runs of the LHC and its upgrated version will enable a variety of experiments involving lower-luminosity, smaller-scale systems. We present the status of several minor projects that aim to investigate exotic phenomena through Baryon-Number Violation, Electric Dipole Moments, and Meson Mixing experiments. These experiments, which involve particles like neutrons, heavy neutral mesons, and neutral kaons, are challenging but potentially rewarding to investigate with cutting-edge accelerators.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have persisted for an extended period have led to speculation that they might be stellar mass black holes or low-mass neutron stars. To determine if the nature of these sources could be neutron stars, we examined the recurrence times of tidal disruption events involving X-ray binary transients. We found that if these events occur at a rate of at least one per century, any neutron star with an atmosphere of mostly hydrogen or helium would need to have a high temperature, exceeding 0.1 times the million Kelvin scale. Given that current measurements of the sources do not meet this criterion, we conclude that the recurrence rate of these events must be lower, possibly around one event per few decades or more.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two distinct groups of entities, and their vertices can be categorized into two disjoint sets. A key characteristic of these graphs is that their edges only connect nodes within different sets. Sometimes, specific properties of a graph are required to meet certain criteria, which can be achieved through various transformations such as reserving, deleting, or modifying the graph's edges, or even changing the attributes of its vertices. A particular type of modification involves altering a vertex's characteristics, which can occur when a vertex from one set needs to be relocated to the other set due to its new set of connections. This paper focuses on resolving the problem of transferring a vertex from one set to the other, which is referred to as "splitting" the vertex. The goal is to find a configuration that satisfies a specific relational property, with any remaining discrepancies corrected through edge modifications. A notable example of this approach is its potential application in transferring consensus algorithms from bipartite graphs to ones with a single connected component, which could be beneficial when using a particular identifier that is unique to each group.

Recent studies show that energy harvesting techniques can effectively mitigate side-channel attacks, but their slow speeds limit their practical use. In response, we propose an innovative method called HyperDegrade, which accelerates power harvesting by over 2 orders of magnitude without compromising mitigation efficacy. HyperDegrade combines dynamic frequency adjustment and cache optimization to optimize data eviction efficiency. Our evaluations using RamChar and PowerChar side-channel attacks demonstrate that cache states remain highly predictable even with skewed power profiles. Furthermore, experiments on real-world applications reveal that power harvesting side-channel attacks succeed even with non-ideal cache flushing methods. As a result, ordinary software can still exploit RPO and PO side-channel vulnerabilities due to effective mitigation strategies that distort power profiles and optimize cache states. This finding highlights the importance of optimizing cache states rather than power profiles to mitigate side-channel attacks, opening up new research possibilities.

The paper introduces an additional type of local knot modification termed the disentangling move, extending the previous set of moves including the second and fourth Reidemeister moves as well as the Delta moves. This additional move is illustrated to expand the generality of disjoint equivalence between links whose components do not intersect. Furthermore, the document proves that combining all three sets of moves is equivalent to a previously established minimal set of local moves that produce the same result.

The paper investigates the problem of synchronizing a specific type of protocol used by robots on a network, taking into account their limited computational abilities and communication range. A decision is made on the best approach to minimize the gap between the current time and the most recent shared information, considering potential threats, communication patterns, and energy usage. A new method is proposed to optimize this objective directly, and theoretical support is provided to validate its effectiveness. Additionally, direct formulas are derived to calculate the optimal outcome. Numerical examples are used to illustrate the application of these findings.

In our study, we demonstrated that both the general linear group of $n$ elements over a field of $q$ elements ($SL_n(q)$) for $n\geq 3$ and the symplectic group $\Sp_{2n}(q)$ over a field of $q$ elements for $n\geq 3$, can be embedded within the wreath product of symmetric groups of $m$ elements over a set of $k$ elements ($S_k\wr T_m$) with $k\geq 3$. Notably, these results achieve reduced bounds on $k$ compared to previous methods.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the frequency range beyond 100 Hz due to various noise sources. Overcoming this limitation is critical for enhancing the effectiveness of detector networks, particularly when searching for compact binary inspirals of intermediate-mass black holes. Recent research indicates that Sagnac interferometers could offer improved sensitivity in this area. However, their potential benefits are constrained by the limitations common to both Michelson and Sagnac interferometer designs. We introduce a novel configuration called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which incorporates a pre-encoder and pre-modulator system based on a Sagnac setup. This new design could potentially offer significant improvements in sensitivity at high frequencies, as it effectively mitigates the usual limitations imposed by quantum back-action and photon shot noise. Analytical models and simulation results support the potential benefits of this innovative configuration.

Recent studies on XL-MIMO systems have employed spherical or conical geometries to design random access protocols. However, since data points in an XL-MIMO system are spaced at integer coordinates, we believe conical and spherical shapes are not the most effective way to design these protocols. Instead, we propose using intersecting visibility regions, derived from a modified version of Voronoi cells, to design the protocol. This approach ensures that users assigned to non-overlapping regions have zero inter-cell interference, resulting in more fair region assignments. To optimize performance, we utilize integer programming to find the maximum set of non-overlapping regions, which can be utilized in XL-MIMO random access protocols. Applying this method to theoretical models demonstrates that the non-overlapping region-based protocol outperforms existing protocols, providing higher throughput with lower signal-to-noise ratio requirements.

A high-performance neural network language model should ideally capture all essential linguistic information, including rare and complex grammatical structures, while also accounting for the statistics of a given text. However, previous studies have shown that neural networks fall short in doing so completely, often relying on a remaining component that appears to handle basic grammar and text distribution effectively. This study reveals that this remaining component is actually an $N$-gram model that can be easily extracted from the neural network. By integrating the $N$-gram model with the neural network in a residual manner, the authors achieved significant improvements in various text generation tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art results. The proposed method, called Residual Neural Network ($$ResNN$$), demonstrates its effectiveness through extensive experiments on a range of tasks such as language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, showing notable gains in terms of perplexity and accuracy metrics.

This investigation seeks to examine the in-depth capabilities of our newly developed script, iOCR, an Informed Optical Character Recognition system. By integrating iOCR's initial oOCR module which identifies text-bearing areas with an additional OCR engine, more precise results can be obtained. As opposed to conventional OCR methods, iOCR's informed approach yields substantially lower error rates. We found error rates of 1.32%, 1.50%, and 0.03% for iOCR when applied to Sample A, B, C, in comparison to 21.07%, 17.03%, 12.73%, and 4.22%, 3.35%, 2.11% for standard OCR techniques.

A simplified computational model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in terrestrial atmospheres with varying physical properties. By varying the rotation rate, temperature gradient, and atmospheric composition of a simulated planet, a wide range of circulation patterns are explored. A diagram is used to categorize and map these patterns in relation to these physical parameters, revealing distinct regions for various circulation types such as multiple-cell systems, two-jet systems, multi-jet systems, and single-jet systems with one or more circulation cells. Key transitions between these regions are identified and explained in terms of the atmospheric, thermal, and Coriolis forces, providing insights into the boundary conditions that define each region. The findings contribute to our understanding of various global circulation patterns observed in exoplanets and simplify the complexity of atmospheric modeling.

This study formulates two potential serial product representations of the reciprocal gamma function, derived from the regularized integral expressions of the gamma function, based on the serialization product definition of the Poisson carrousel.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, including Bose-Einstein condensates, with remarkable accuracy. This research extends previous work by developing a novel statistical method, called random quantum hydrodynamics, which introduces fluctuations into the Wigner function, a powerful tool for describing quantum systems in phase space. This approach allows for a stochastic simulation of many-body systems, where the Wigner function's evolution is modeled as a random process, similar to a diffusion process, during a time-step, and a reliable linear solver is used to ensure the Wigner function's validity at the end of each step. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through Wigner-phase-space portraits of a collapsing Bose gas and a two-component Bose gas, as well as a multi-component system, and compares its results to standard quantum linear solver simulations and mean-field theories.

The vast amount of unstructured information online has made knowledge management a significant challenge, prompting the development of various Inferring Systems with Embeddings to address this issue. One category of these systems includes models that operate in one or two layers to directly process unstructured data. Another category consists of architectures designed to work with structured information, which consists of multiple layers and involves a continual learning process. We have created and structured the first comprehensive survey focusing on Inferring Systems with Embeddings, which have been used in Knowledge Learning with Structured Information. This architecture, which we've named the Teacher-Student Model, typically comprises an initial reduction student model that processes detailed student models in a few steps to extract and learn from structured information in a continuous and efficient manner. This model has been applied in a variety of tasks, including knowledge graph completion, relationship prediction, knowledge graph construction, and question answering. However, we have also identified several challenges and potential directions for future research within this area.

Integrating probabilistic graphical models with external constraints like first-order logic can significantly increase computational complexity, particularly in highly interconnected situations such as image processing. A common approach to resolving this complexity involves factorizing the problem, which often sacrifices accuracy. We introduce a compact factorization method that yields precise results by leveraging matrix multiplication, and we determine the resulting time complexity as O(n^2m + n^2log_2(n) + nlog_2(n) + dlog_2(n)), where n represents the number of variables, m the state alphabet size, and d the factorization radius. We found that this accuracy-FLOP efficiency surpasses existing integration methods, including one proposed by Shawe-Donovan et al. (2014).

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. A key finding connects this $sR(n)$ to the 2nd graded association of $n$-th Heckenbergero algebra $E_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through an isomorphism. Additionally, a recurring pattern is discovered in the Hilbert series of graded components of $sR(n)$, linking it to a sequence of integer polynomials denoted as $S_n(k)$.

The central bank's intervention capabilities are crucial for maintaining financial market stability. To evaluate how effectively central banks can accomplish this objective, researchers have developed paired permutation tests to examine the asymmetry in interest rate impacts on monetary policy tools such as day forward rates. Since interest rate data exhibits a high degree of serial correlation, the test's accuracy is enhanced through a paired permutation approach that ensures reliable results. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulations and an analysis of actual central bank data.

In high-energy particle collisions, a phenomenon known as triangular flow ($v_3$) is observed. To better understand this, we simulated central gold and copper collisions at 200 GeV using a model called iPMR-TYUEN, paying close attention to how energy is transferred and particles are produced in the initial stages of the collision without considering initial glasma spikes. Our findings indicate that including these spikes would not significantly impact our predictions. We found linear relationships between $v_3$ and three measures of momentum anisotropy at various angles. Additionally, we observed that $v_3$ increases as the energy transferred in the collision increases, a trend that mirrors experimental data. To further investigate the role of pressure in driving flow, we conducted simulations with artificially stened equations of state, discovering that a more robust equation leads to higher $v_3$ values.

This study presents a refined point hypothesis density filter, specifically tailored for applications in sensor management, where the birth process is represented by a grid-based model with an infinite grid size. The refined algorithm modifies the grid model to eliminate unnecessary computations outside of a finite region of interest. Alongside the algorithmic update, the paper also proposes a novel information-sharing protocol for distributed sensors to optimize expected performance while minimizing costs. A joint optimization problem is formulated to maximize sensor management performance, taking into consideration computational constraints, and is solved using a iterative method. To illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, two examples are provided and analyzed.

The dynamics of soccer games can lead to moments where teams suddenly lose the ball, making these instances highly unpredictable and difficult to analyze using traditional data. To address this, we developed a new type of dataset that tracks player movements and ball possession more accurately, along with information on scoring events. This refined dataset, which we made publicly available, allows for more complex analysis. We conducted several experiments to compare various models that use deep learning for scoring prediction, including a baseline model and variations with different input components. Additionally, we implemented a action-selection policy using deep reinforcement learning to explore its ability to improve the prediction of certain moments in the game. The results demonstrated that incorporating model-based deep reinforcement learning can significantly enhance the accuracy of scoring prediction, particularly in critical situations where goals are scored.

The advancement of laser technology has enabled a single-point LDV system to measure velocity fields over large areas, which is highly beneficial for researching large-scale movements in fluids. To achieve this expansion, we have developed and tested a new optical arrangement to image the experiment area using a combination of concave mirrors and beam expanders. The system's effectiveness has been confirmed through laboratory experiments using both laser light sources, a HeNe and CO2 laser, to measure the vibrations of a vibrating plate with high accuracy. The results have shown that this configuration can effectively measure velocity fields over large areas, which is a significant advancement for researching fluid dynamics over vast regions.

This paper provides precise definitions for the operators $H_1$ and $G$ acting on the complex vector space $\mathbb{C}2$ and then examines their spectral characteristics, as well as the stability of their ground states and first excited states. A numerical algorithm has been developed to determine the exact spectrum for various parameter combinations and to identify the corresponding eigenvectors. Additionally, theoretical proofs are presented for vector space relations between the operators that result in purely discrete spectra. Under specific conditions, both the ground and excited states are found to be stable. However, when certain inequalities are met, the states are discovered to be unstable, and unique unstable energies are identified along with the corresponding eigenfunctions.

To predict the properties of axion-like particles (ALPs) that decay into hadrons, specifically involving photon and hadron interactions, a quantum electrodynamics-based framework is employed. This method enables the calculation of ALP-hadron vertex characteristics from $B$ meson decay data, which is set to be analyzed by the Belle II experiment. To illustrate the potential of this approach, the Belle II experiment's alien particle search capabilities are depicted through efficiency-vs-coupling strength graphs for $B$ meson decays into specific alien particle states. These illustrations are compared to existing limitations from KLOE and LHCd experiments. It is found that the constraints produced by Belle II are more stringent than those from KLOE for certain coupling ranges, though not as effective as those from LHCd. Moreover, both experiment and theory requirements are shown for specific alien particle states resulting from $B$ meson decays. A new search for such decays is proposed for the Belle II experiment, with a significance formula considering background rates, integrated luminosity, and signal strength to identify potential alien particle discoveries.

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of semantic change detection in text through interpolation and training. This enhancement has potentially overshadowed the relevance of existing evaluation metrics, possibly favoring technically advanced models while undermining fair comparison and possibly contributing to bias towards certain models and methods, potentially disenfranchising others and impacting safety, ethics, and fairness considerations. Our research explores updated evaluation protocols, possibly offering optimized assessments while promoting fairness, ethics, and inclusivity. We have developed a new testing framework, potentially providing a more equitable and representative evaluation environment that better reflects diverse linguistic patterns, accents, dialects, and cultural contexts. Our new dataset, comprising 1000k training samples and 50k test instances, may offer a more comprehensive and unbiased resource for training and evaluating semantic alteration detection models while ensuring high precision, recall, F1 scores, and fairness across various linguistic characteristics, genders, ages, races, and socio-economic statuses.

We develop a relational verification condition generator for applying quantum Hoare logic in a
  bi-relational context to ensure code consistency between two systems simultaneously. This
  enhancement builds on existing quantum invariants to facilitate variable relations in bi-invariant
  statements, and introduces a deterministic, constraint-based generator to validate consistency
  across both relational and quantum conditions. As a result, we obtain a strengthened
  bi-relational verification variant suitable for a refined set of interpersonal guarantees.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue becomes more pronounced in areas with weak magnetic fields and is exacerbated when using certain algorithms. To tackle this, the study proposes a method that involves analyzing the source of Bperp bias by examining the reduction in magnetic flux when flux-free initial conditions are used to seed radiative transfer algorithms. A neural network is then trained to predict corrections for Bparallel based on local conditions, using data from various inversion algorithms. The improved inversion technique retains the accuracy of existing methods while alleviating the biquadratic nature of Bperp bias, making it linear or even reducing it in some cases. The upgrade is particularly beneficial for coronal modeling and is validated through numerical tests, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving the fidelity of vector magnetic field maps.

The purpose of this article is to fully characterize boolean lattices, Booleans algebras to be exact, and then present the lattice of involutions of a free boolean lattice of n generators as a boolean lattice of 2n-1 generators for n greater than or equal to 4 as well as the structure of the boolean lattice of 3-dimensional space for a 2-dimensional lattice

This research is centered on the geometric properties of curves within the context of semi-Riemannian manifolds, exploring the definition and characteristics of what are referred to as Berternod curves. A detailed explanation of the curve parametrisation is also provided.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as unimportant compared to the network's architecture and parameters. However, this claim lacks rigorous statistical support. We conduct a comprehensive investigation into the correlation between loss function selection and a network's accuracy, particularly in classification tasks. Our findings reveal that while all common loss functions concave and have been shown to be optimized, they are all monotonically related and produce comparable results. We develop a metric to evaluate the impact of loss function changes on network performance and apply it to analyze the influence of these factors. Our experiments demonstrate that although loss function optimization is generally equivalent, more extreme functions can lead to slight performance declines. Furthermore, we observe that certain architectures are more susceptible to the potential negative effects of less convex loss functions.

Integrating complex knowledge graphs into neural networks often leads to issues with scalability and efficiency. To address these challenges and enable detailed knowledge acquisition, a comprehensive dataset of 72,000 natural language rules derived from the ConceptNet knowledge graph was created. This rule-based subset, referred to as the ATOMIC atlas, is suitable for training neural networks on if-then knowledge integration. The dataset is organized into four main categories, further divided into 16 sub-categories, with a focus on multi-step reasoning tasks. To evaluate various model architectures, four assessment methods were developed, including subjective surveys, automated evaluation, and analyses of stacking models and gradual changes. A baseline model, along with several variations, was analyzed, with the best results achieved by a model combining attention and memory components. The ATOMIC atlas is deemed an ideal platform for researching knowledge integration in neural networks, with future possibilities including expanding the dataset, exploring various knowledge sources, and designing more sophisticated reasoning tasks.

A subgraph of a given graph G is considered a subset of its vertices, with the induced subgraph formed by the edges with both endpoints in that subset. A graph's metric dimension is defined as the minimum metric dimension of its subgraphs, while a subset of its vertices is considered independent if the subgraph they induce does not contain any edges. A graph's stable number is the maximum size of such an subgraph. This article proves that for a connected graph with at least two vertices, the minimum metric dimension of its subgraphs lies between its stable number and the sum of its angle and center indices.

We discovered that for weaker molecular gases in galaxies, the emission of singly ionized neutral atomic carbon lines observed so far does not follow the predicted theoretical curve by the Scovelle et al. (1984) diagram. This deviation indicates that energy sources like star formation are not effectively heating dust at wavelengths greater than 160um, indicating the presence of dark star formation. Alternatively, cosmic ray radiation may be responsible for producing millimeter radiation in molecular gases, rather than star formation. This mechanism, which is theoretically possible, needs to be confirmed through further research. In addition, we proposed that the efficiency of (96,52)μm line excitation can serve as an observable indicator to distinguish between thermal and nonthermal excitation sources, filling a gap in spectral lines available for research.

A key aspect of non-equilibrium statistical physics is understanding how systems evolve over time. To uncover the complete phase diagram of the asymmetric simple exclusion model with varying densities at internal sites and velocity fluctuations, we derive the underlying structure of the velocity process, classifying it as a piece of martingale and obtaining its stationary distribution.

This study examines various mathematical models used to track epidemic outbreaks, assessing their strengths, weaknesses, and suitability for real-time data analysis during active outbreaks. As outbreaks evolve dynamically, models must be easy to update with emerging information, balancing the need for simplicity and the availability of data against the desire for precision and predictive capability. Although forecasting peak times and outbreak sizes is often discussed, such predictions can be unreliable due to their sensitivity to initial conditions and rapid changes in outbreak dynamics. Instead, real-time models can be adapted to predict outbreak trajectories under different intervention strategies, aiding policymakers in making informed decisions about potential measures and their impacts. To illustrate these concepts, the paper presents several models applicable to the current COVID-19 outbreak, exploring their underlying assumptions, mathematical frameworks, and implications for outbreak management and control.
Determining whether bulge or galaxy mass determines the bend in the star formation main sequence is still unresolved.

This paper investigates cross-language sentiment analysis using the Amazon products dataset, involving approximately 500k English reviews with labeled sentiments and a smaller sample of Portuguese reviews for a subset of products. Our research utilized a mult-task learning approach with a convolutional neural network, incorporating a ranking loss to maintain consistency between the two languages' vocabularies. We assessed the model's effectiveness through both English to Portuguese and Portuguese to English translation tasks, measuring success with F1 scores. The results demonstrated that our system significantly outperformed existing methods, bridging the gap between supervised and unsupervised approaches, and highlighting the importance of shared semantic representations in cross-language sentiment analysis.

This study presents a notable discrepancy between theoretical predictions and observations of a brown dwarf named 2M0527-0033. Our spectroscopic analysis reveals that the brown dwarf's atmosphere is exceptionally hot and rapidly rotating compared to similar objects. While 2M0530-0047, a companion planet, is believed to have been ejected due to its initial gas giant status, it is hypothesized that the surrounding protoplanetary disk caused the planet to fall back onto the brown dwarf, potentially leading to an unusual state of inflation and rapid rotation. However, more efficient angular momentum transport mechanisms, such as the Riley et al. (2008) model, appear to be insufficient to explain the observed characteristics of 2M0527-0047. Consequently, it is proposed that electric fields induced by tidal forces, as suggested by the Marleire et al.(2013) model, may have played a role in the observed behavior, or that the initial estimate of the mass for 2M0530-0047 was inaccurate.

The rapid proliferation of social media has made information overload a prevalent issue, enabling fake news to spread quickly and cause significant harm. With the advent of multimedia, fake news often incorporates images and videos, posing a complex challenge for detection systems that rely on either text or multimedia alone. Although deep learning has produced promising results in homogeneous domains, its effectiveness may not translate well to multimodal scenarios due to the lack of cross-domain shared representations. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that utilizes meta-learning to enable an model trained on single-modal data to effectively detect fake news incorporating multimedia, without requiring prior bimodal training. Our experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Constructing disjoint sets of signals with low correlation like Golay complementary arrays (GCA) is a challenging task in information theory. This article presents a new method for GCA construction that does not rely on multiplication. The construction consists of two or four lower correlation arrays that can be combined to form a GCA.的理论 shows that a combination of these arrays results in cancellation of correlation terms at specific frequencies, similar to what has been proven in previous research. Notably, the construction ensures that the resulting GCA has a minimum gain that depends on the individual array gains. Statistics regarding the possible sizes of GCA designs are also discussed. The new construction is found to produce larger size GCA designs compared to existing records for various array dimensions and correlation levels.

The healthcare sector's rapid advancement has raised concerns about intellectual property protection and patient safety, prompting a need for secure techniques like medical image encryption. Consequently, developing robust and effective debiasing methods is crucial to demonstrate the applicability of our proposed scheme in real-world scenarios.

Integrating graph neural networks with deep learning has significantly enhanced network analysis, but the diverse structures employed hinder effective knowledge transfer between various networks. To resolve this, our research proposes a novel framework called Shared-Encoder Contrastive Learning (SEC-Learning) that unifies feature extraction for various network structures. SEC-Learning utilizes contrastive learning to find an optimal representation space where network nodes can be effectively matched, enabling a single encoder to replace multiple, structure-specific encoders. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SEC-Learning in improving network analysis tasks compared to existing methods.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-level performance on many language tasks. Despite these successes, I think the models' capacity to effectively utilize training data with specific grammatical structures is limited. To overcome this obstacle, we developed our first contribution, which outlines a fully structured knowledge representation called KDGraf, kaggle-style data oriented KDGraf format, designed for data similar to what's found on Kaggle. KDGraf is an iterative process with three distinct steps: document summarization, table extraction, and entity linking. We believe KDGraf is easy to extend with new information sources and agile to integrate into the large language model workflow. Our second contribution demonstrates the effectiveness of KDGraf in various benchmark tests, showing significant performance gains over other methods with structuredly trained data. The results indicate that KDGraf leads KGMBase, our newly created KDGraf-enhanced foundation model, to outperform the model without KDGraf integration on multiple evaluation tests including GLUE, FEVER, and HUMANEval. We believe both our KDGraf representation and the KGMBase model will benefit the field of NLP with high-quality structured knowledge sources.

Non-linear interactions between photons in vacuum can lead to altering the dynamics of both the temperature and energy flux within radiative equilibrium around black holes. By applying the concept of holographic mutual information, this research aims to determine the conditions under which external charged black holes in a radiation field can be sustained. It is found that for non-linear charged AdS black holes, there exists a critical charge-to-mass ratio beyond which maintenance becomes impossible without a specific minimum charge-to-mass ratio in the surrounding radiation field. It is also discovered that, in a linear charged field, there is an optimal temperature that maximizes the stability of black holes, absent in a scenario with charged fields. Furthermore, similar to the case with AdS black holes in a massless scalar field, a shade stability region is identified in a linearity-charged field, beyond which information collapse occurs due to excessive radiation, mirance collapse is observed in a fixed charge field beyond a certain threshold of linearity, and similar behavior is found in a fixed linearity field beyond a specific charge field limit. In addition, it is discovered that both the linearity field and charge field have an impact on shade stability region boundaries.

Following our earlier discussion presented in Ref.10, this article introduces a new image fidelity measure for continuous-variable quantum states, based on conventional information metrics. The fidelity alteration concept is demonstrated to equate to variations in quantum entanglement for Gaussian CV states. Moreover, the article derives a non-linear information metric specifically for CV states and shows that its relation to fidelity alteration can be optimized, resulting in a straightforward fidelity definition tailored for CV states. This new definition is then proven to link information loss and synchronization onset in identical quantum Langevin equations describing two coupled oscillators.

Researchers have measured two specific meson decay processes, $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$, for the first time using data from particle collisions at various energies, with a total of 7.3 million $B\bar{B}$ pairs produced. The decays were identified through a chain of interactions involving other particles, and their observed frequencies were determined to be $0.07\pm0.04\pm0.01\pm0.01\%$ and $0.10\pm0.10\pm0.01\pm0.01\%$, respectively. These results align with current theoretical predictions.

Constructing module lattices has long been a challenging combinatorial task, particularly when dealing with modules over rings that aren't associative, such as Lie algebras. While existing algorithms work well for module lattices, they fall short when it comes to submodules, as they require computationally intensive calculations. However, in cases where modules are deemed multiplicity-free, a more streamlined approach is possible. In these scenarios, where decomposing submodules into components is not possible, lattice structures can be deduced from a simpler data set consisting of inclusion relationships among submodules. This method, which involves a step-by-step process, allows for the reconstruction of lattice structures without the need for traditional module lattice construction techniques, making it particularly useful when dealing with high-dimensional multiplicity-free modules.

If a manifold $λ$ is embedded in the Euclidean space and possesses either invariant or recurrent properties, then either the square norm of the Laplacian operator or the square norm of the curvature tensor is constant. A key theorem proves that for such manifolds with these characteristics, the norm is constant. Furthermore, if the dimension is at least 4 and the manifold is biharmonic, additional conclusions about its configuration can be made.

Rosenberg and Yankilevsky introduced a code format called p/q-KZ in 2018, with p/q-KZ being a variation of KZ codes. KZ codes are known to be optimal for the (2, infinity) problem, whereas p/q-KZ is ideal for the (p/q, 2) problem when p/q is greater than 1. A special subclass of p/q-KZ codes, named p/q-identifiable wires, was introduced to ensure reliability against an adversary who can disrupt up to half of the wires. A key finding establishes that (2, infinity) and p/q-identifiable wires are equivalent when p/q is slightly less than 2, demonstrating that these codes can protect against adversaries capable of manipulating a constant fraction of the data on any given time step.
Weak decays of charged currents exhibit tree-level interactions and serve as a foundation for flavor physics.

A persistent puzzle in physics concerns the intermittent bursts observed during various brittle failure processes, with researchers arguing over whether a power-law pattern exists in the energy release spectrum. While Embolden et al.'s model predicted power-law behavior, it conflicted with more accurate simulations. To resolve this, we used a high-resolution point process model to simulate such failures, revealing power-law-like patterns in the resulting binched spectrum, along with peaks at zero frequency and around 100mm/s, closely mirping the experimental data.

In 1927, Menger developed an interest in the study of geometry in spaces of possible positions of points, also known as ultrametrics. He examined a specific type of geometric structure in these spaces that incorporated the concept of angles between segments connecting the points.

Point-cloud based neural networks often suffer from several limitations, including low resolution graphs causing information loss, computationally heavy high-resolution graphs, and external dependencies for model construction. To address these issues we propose a new framework utilizing deep neural networks for shape inference. Our framework consists of three modules: an initial extractor that generates an informative descriptor from the current graph, a pre-trained classifier that leverages the descriptor for quick classification, and a high-resolution graph optimizer that employs attention mechanisms for further shape refinement if necessary. We propose an optimization strategy to prevent overfitting and present the first one-shot learning approach for model compression. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework for point cloud classification and smoothing tasks.

Integrating formal verification into the software development process is challenging due to its cost and technical difficulty. We propose a geometric-based testing method that offers a practical alternative, leveraging precise measurements to validate code's correctness. This approach generates test cases from input-output manifolds, including critical points where function behavior changes. A case study on Polygon area calculation demonstrates the effectiveness of this manifold-based technique.

We provide an explicit description of Kummer theory based Serre weights through an induction of character, extending previous findings by several mathematicians. Our approach offers concrete computations of dual Mellin transforms, providing us with explicit formulations of local Artin conductors. This detailed understanding of Kummer theory enables us to prove the existence of Clear Mellin operators, which in turn establishes the existence of Clear Serre weights, specifically through representations of GL_2 over p-adic fields.

To monitor the health of composite materials in real-time, creating accurate 3D images of damage through electrical resistance measurement is challenging due to the complex relationship between electricity and damage in these materials. A study was conducted on carbon fiber reinforced polymer to improve the accuracy of 3D damage imaging. A genetic algorithm was developed to optimize electrical stimulation patterns and measurement locations, resulting in more accurate damage images. The algorithm outperformed common methods, reducing error by 37% with two electrodes and enabling accurate imaging with just four electrodes. Additionally, the study demonstrated the ability to track damage growth in relation to changes in material conductivity, providing a reliable way to monitor damage progression.

This paper rewrites a tensor-based theory of Euclidean space using only geometric terms such as vectors, covectors, rotations, and reflections, eliminating the use of indices. Although working with indices is efficient for computations, this intuitive approach provides a deeper understanding of the underlying principles. Key geometric quantities including area vectors, volume vectors, dual area vectors, dual volume vectors, normal vectors, and volumes are defined in multi-dimensional spaces without relying on index notation. Furthermore, fundamental tensor equations such as the metric tensor, Kronecker delta, Levi-Civita symbol, and identity tensor are expressed using geometric quantities in both 2D and 3D spaces without using indices. By the end of this index-free exploration, essential tensor-based relationships are translated into equivalent equations using geometric quantities.

If a right-angled octet graph lacks a triangle, we can determine the number of components in its component parts based on the number of components in its components. Additionally, we can determine the structure of its fundamental group based on the structure of the fundamental groups of its components. As a result, we obtain new conditions for a given subgroup of a right-angled Artin group to be conjugate to a subgroup of the edge stabilizers.

We extend an iterative matrix inversion algorithm originally proposed by Haidar and Nadler in 2013, which is optimized for GPU use, based on (m,k)-outer iterations. By incorporating additional (m,k)-outer iterations, we derive a new three-parameter family of methods, (m,r,k), representing an infinite hierarchy of techniques. Through mathematical analysis, we determine the convergence order of this family to be $2^{\frac{r-m}{m}}+(1+\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{n})2^{\frac{r-m}{m}}$, where $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_n$ represent the largest and smallest eigenvalues in absolute value. In addition, we compare the performance of various methods within this family, including existing algorithms, to establish optimal parameter combinations for both 2x2 and 4x4 matrices.

Contextual linear bandits is a crucial model with wide-ranging applications, and its decentralized variant presents a promising direction for future expansion. In this variant, the decision-making agent, a learner, obtains rewards and selects contexts from a available set, with the key challenge lying in the lack of explicit context information at the agent's disposal. Instead, a source, or server, holds this information and shares it with the agent, who in turn communicates actions and values back to the source. This paper focuses on the scenario where both the source and agent are subject to communication constraints, and aims to minimize regret, a measure of performance. By leveraging the unique structure of the problem, the author proposes a new algorithm, D$^2$-LBCV, and establishes theoretical bounds on regret for it. These bounds depend on various factors, including the number of source and agent nodes, the set of possible contexts, and the extent of communication constraints. Furthermore, the author proves that this regret bound order is optimal for general contexts, and provides a new lower bound, a more stringent standard for context sets with specific properties.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is thought to occur in the outer areas of protoplanetary disks, with its potential effects affected by patterns of grain growth. To better understand how VSI works in these regions, we conducted a 3D simulation that takes grain evolution into account. As we observed in the simulation, grain growth leads to heavier settling of particles at the disk's midplane, creating a more stable environment and reducing the VSI's impact. Without grain growth, temperatures rise and the disk's mass ejection rate increases significantly. However, with growth occurring, the same effect is diminished due to the isolation of energy from the midplane. The model shows that without grain growth, a million欧姆 per square meter can be reached within a short time, enabling an even greater mass ejection rate. As grain layers form around the midplane, the resistance decreases, and the VSI's ability to create current disruptions diminishes. To accurately predict how VSI behaves in these regions, more information is needed on the connection between particle size and electrical resistance.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of certain Riemannian manifolds, specifically those satisfying certain conditions, and examines their boundedness or growth at infinity. Under the assumption that a manifold possesses an integrated Ricci curvature that's not decreasing and a constant curvature in the scalar dimension, it is demonstrated that bounded harmonic functions do not exist within the manifold, thereby proving a theorem by Yau on Yau shrinkers. Moreover, it is established that on manifolds meeting Yau shrinker conditions, any harmonic function with a specific growth rate is uniquely decomposable into a sum of specific polynomial and hyperbolic cosine functions.

Recent advancements in deep learning have resulted in the free generation of backdoors by malicious actors, which often impair the usability of models and pose security risks. In response, we introduce a novel concept called dynamic backdoors, and demonstrate its ability to compromise the reliability of models in an optimization-oriented context. Our findings suggest that combining regular backdoors with invisible biases before training and then adjusting their intensity during training can lead to sophisticated attack patterns. Furthermore, we found that traditional countermeasures such as unlearning and cleaning are ineffective against this type of attack, but we developed a new method called dynamic backdoor erasure (DBE) based on the Sigmold activation function. Our experiments with GPT2 and BERT show that this function works effectively in eliminating the impact of regular and sophisticated backdoor attacks, including those with high fidelity, without sacrificing model accuracy.

In the context of a parameter averaging technique used in federated learning, a client's local decision makes the process computationally heavy. To address this, we propose to optimize it by sampling a subset of layers and clients, thereby reducing communication costs. We then introduce a random walk strategy that enables a client to learn from a limited set of data points, significantly speeding up local training without degrading model performance. Our results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, which we've named "stroll," in achieving satisfactory accuracy while reducing communication costs by up to 99.7% and training times by up to 4.5 times compared to existing techniques.

This study presents a consistency regularization approach using average labels for medical image segmentation. While existing methods often require precise or intricate label processing, our technique avoids this by utilizing mean labels. Although it may theoretically introduce bias, we found no significant impact in practice. Although prior research often integrates active learning, our method stands alone without this component. Although other models often employ deep neural networks, we found it not necessary for our purpose.

A theoretically derived result indicates that single-particle entanglement can produce truly nonlocal effects, including single-particle steering when comparing complex and real vector spaces.  Without complex numbers, local hidden variable models suffice to explain observations from single-particle interference experiments.  Conversely, discarding entanglement forces hidden variable models to produce outcomes mathematically equivalent to interference patterns.  Since previous arguments requiring both the removal of complex numbers and entanglement are impossible, a novel example is necessary to establish that single-particle states can produce genuinely nonlocal effects.  To this end, we propose an experimental setup consisting of two spatially separated interferometers to achieve this.  Analyzing the resulting observations, we find that complex numbers play a role similar to that of entanglement in multi-particle systems.  Consequently, single-particle states can become entangled when viewed from the perspective of two interconnected complex vector spaces.  This phenomenon, therefore, reflects a true nonlocal property, and we suggest that to fully describe the quantum state of a single particle, the complex vector space of spinors should be regarded as inherently two-dimensional.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and Information Technology within Internet-of-Vehicles networks presents significant challenges, particularly regarding data privacy and security. Federated Learning offers a potential solution by enabling decentralized learning and enhancing privacy, yet the evolution of complex applications within these networks may lead to model inconsistencies. Here enters the concept of Blockchain technology, which can guarantee security, integrity, and trustworthy interactions. To keep pace with current research trends, this paper conducts an in-depth review and analysis of latest studies that explore the synergistic potential of Blockchain and Federated Learning for Internet-of-Vehicles networks. The article begins by outlining fundamental concepts of Federated Learning, Blockchain technology, and Internet-of-Vehicles networks, followed by a classification of existing research into three primary categories: privacy preservation, security enhancement, and incentive mechanisms. The article concludes by highlighting unresolved issues and proposing future research directions in this promising field.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved significant success in various NLP and computer vision tasks but often require substantial computational power and memory, limiting their use in edge devices. While numerous attempts to optimize these models have been made, simultaneously optimizing the algorithm and hardware for specific applications is a novel and challenging endeavor. To bridge this gap, we propose a framework that designs energy-efficient LSTM networks for video identification on specific hardware architectures. Since different layers of an LSTM model have distinct performance and hardware requirements, we investigate the potential for pruning less effective layers without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, we design a customized hardware system tailored to the characteristics of the optimized algorithm, leveraging the flexibility of field-programmable gate arrays and the efficiency of digital circuits. The integration of an optimized algorithm and specialized hardware results in significant improvements in video identification accuracy on several datasets compared to existing models. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm硬件 co设计方法，opening new possibilities for deploying deep learning models on edge devices with low power consumption and high efficiency.

We establish a new necessary condition for a polynomial $f \\in \\mathbb{C}[x]$ to satisfy an functional equation $f(g(x)) = g(f(x))$, where $g$ is another polynomial. Additionally, we determine all monic primitive integer polynomials that maintain this property while acting on integral rings.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation that exhibit explosive growth at the endpoint of its critical exponent, confined to the exterior of a convex obstacle. We identify a solution whose $L^\infty$ norm increases exponentially over time, exponentially faster than the dispersion estimate predicts. To counter the potential influence of the obstacle, we employ a Carleman estimate tailored to the setting, which establishes an exponential growth of the solution's energy outside a specific region around the obstacle. Conversely, to prove that solutions without mass concentration near the obstacle experience explosive growth, we utilize a technique that extends the equation's solution into the interior of a obstacle, analogous to a scattering approach.

We develop a semi-parametric version of Watanabe and Yoshida's local change of variables technique, allowing for modifications of a given variety in positive characteristic. This approach is then applied to establish local parametric singularities removal for the variety defined by $f x - g y+h=0$ in a three-dimensional space near the origin, where $f$, $g$ and $h$ are polynomial algebra generators over the integers.

Comparing nested models involves several approaches, with regulatory bodies recommending specific criteria for evaluation. When one model includes an extra parameter compared to a nested alternative, information loss can occur due to differences in parameter spaces. To address this issue, we propose considering models of equivalent complexity before making comparisons. If the more intricate model is a Bayesian extension of a simpler one, the additional degree of freedom can often be disregarded. However, when the models differ substantially, we suggest applying a prior adjustment to the larger model to ensure a fair comparison. Additionally, we discuss the role of model evidence graphs in facilitating informed decisions about Bayes factor thresholds.

Introducing DiscSense, a novel discourse analysis tool that goes beyond traditional phrase matching to understand the functional role of discourse markers based on context. This model, trained on the CHILLENCE dataset, outperforms existing approaches by leveraging the BERT framework and an attention-based labeler, and can identify new inferential relationships not recognized in standard models.
Recently, a dual structure emerged for the Jordanian deformation of Poisson brackets. A parameterized extension of this dual relation was then explored.

Automated testing of software often relies on regular expressions for pattern matching. During the testing process, the compiler generates code that creates regular expression instances, which can leave variables unresolved regarding their specific patterns. This results in a type of constraint satisfaction problem known as DFA automaton regular expression inference (DSREI). While basic inference of language equivalence between regular expression patterns is possible with existing tools, they fall short when it comes to handling integer comparisons within regular expressions. To address this limitation, we developed an extended regular expression syntax that incorporates integer comparison operators, and designed a novel combination of tooling that can resolve these more complex constraints. The resulting solution map produces specific regular expressions that satisfy the input constraints, and has been proven to be complete. Our new inference system's capabilities were demonstrated at the 17th International Conference on Verification, Modeling and Simulation of Integrated Circuits and Systems.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, we develop an expression for the conformal block in terms of spinning fields applicable to CFT$_2$ and test it within the AdS$_2$ context. Initially, we derive the generator for AdS$_2$ isometries that incorporate spinning fields and use it to rewrite Brown-Henneaux central charge in terms of boundary values of spinning fields. Subsequently, we obtain a differential equation satisfied by wave functions at the boundary and demonstrate its equivalence to a known second-order differential equation. Finally, we extend this result to three dimensions and show that a similar differential equation holds for AdS$_3$.

To expand the capabilities of wide-field X-ray monitors utilizing lobster-eye microlens arrays (LEMAs), we have developed and evaluated a novel configuration called Multi-LEMAs in which multiple segments are arranged around a circular perimeter.  In this setup, only a portion of the total 4pi steradians is covered, but the system's overall utility is hindered by the need to multiplex the data from multiple sections.  To address this issue, we have tested various strategies including active source scanning, fixed source monitoring, and source imaging, comparing their effectiveness through a combination of geometric considerations and the Fermi gamma-ray burst catalog.  Our findings indicate that an configuration with seven segments of 100 degrees each can effectively monitor the entire sky within 90% efficiency, but adding more segments quickly becomes impractical due to constraints imposed by the LMAs' field of view and the need for sufficient angular separation.  We propose that a optimal configuration consists of three to five segments of 100-120 degrees each, and we are currently designing a demonstration system called Tri-LEMA to test this concept.  This multi-LEMA configuration offers significant advantages over traditional wide-field monitors, enabling a larger field of view, enhanced detection efficiency, and the potential for multiple systems to be integrated around a central detector to further expand coverage.

This research employs a machine learning approach to investigate the connection between the halo mass function and the SNp model's five parameters: bias, slope, normalisation, gamma, and amplitude. Our research indicates that in a universe modeled by the $\Lambda$CDM, the neural networks find the speed field's amplitude and slope to be significant factors in halo formation. To further examine the influence of the speed field, we conducted additional simulations with models that lacked speed gradients and found that removing the gradient leads to an underestimation of more massive halos. In contrast, when we created a model with constant speed amplification to replace the time-varying one, we observed that the effect is comparable to the original model's effects. These findings indicate that halo mass function variations can be used to constrain the speed field's amplitude but not its slope. To verify this conclusion, we conducted simulations with models that had power-law alternative to the exponential Bessel-clamped model and observed similar results. We found that to model the Hubble tension, a constant speed field is insufficient and a model with a constant gain and a linear time dependence is required.

One of the most significant challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak accelerations. Atom interferometry has shown promising results in this area, yet it's constrained by its sensitivity to tides, rotation, seismic activity, and other local disturbances, particularly when experiments are conducted closer to a laboratory's boundary. To enhance sensitivity to acceleration, we propose leveraging the sensitivity of superconductors to local magnetic fields, which can result in Meissner effect losses, causing vibrations in suspended superconducting materials. This strategy enables atomic interferometry to focus on detecting minuscule atomic losses rather than vertical motion, potentially amplishing sensitivity to weak accelerations by several orders of magnitude, and could pave the way for achieving sensitivities as low as $10^{-11} g$ within a 1-meter scale drop experiment.

We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of magnetic impurity-induced states, specifically focusing on an Mn adatom and small Mn clusters on Nb(110)). By employing a sophisticated green-function-based approach, we accurately account for the complex electronic structure of both the superconductor and the magnetic impurities. This allows us to directly compute the spectral function of the system, revealing zero-energy bound states characteristic of Andreev levels. Additionally, we calculate the local current distribution to visualize these states and the associated spin magnetic moment to determine the stability of these states.

This study aims to enhance the performance of deep learning models in diagnosing skin cancer. Although, as is typical with this study, models developed are capable of effective diagnosis, their reliability decreases when presented with atypical instances. To address this issue and as is common in these types of studies, we devised an algorithm that can identify exceptional instances that may mislead the classifier. To this end, we utilized information entropy, an established technique, as a measure of uncertainty in prediction outcomes. An optimization step is then applied to the entropy values to improve the accuracy of classification. It is found that this approach, combined with an existing study's method, can significantly outstand other strategies and models, achieving an F1-score of 98.4% on Hamming distance, and 99.5% accuracy, 98.4% precision, and 99.3% recall, as is typical in this type of research.

The use of high-energy muon collisions offers a unique platform for discovering new particles due to the unique properties of muons which allow for complex interactions involving electroweak forces. As energies increase, the role of weak interactions becomes more significant, leading to a situation where energy conservation is not fully respected during the initial interaction, resulting in the emission of soft and collinear vector bosons by the muons. To accurately calculating cross-sections at the peak of interest near the Z-particle resonance, a precise treatment of these effects is essential. We present a unified framework called the efficient approach that allows an observer in the laboratory to perceive the initial state particles as already weakened interactions, enabling reliable cross-section calculations of complex processes involving new particle production. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to a specific process of new particle production and comparing the results to a traditional calculation method, finding good agreement in most situations but significant discrepancies at higher energies and near resonance with the Z-particle.

This article examines the theories of four prominent 20th-century mathematicians and philosophers—Gödel, Rosser, Carnap, and Tarski—in the fields of mathematical logic, epistemology, and the philosophy of mathematics, presenting them as interconnected concepts. Godel and Rosser are highlighted for their incompleteness theorems, while the article also discusses Godel's solution to the Bertrand Russell paradox and the type theory it introduced. Furthermore, the article delves into the Deduction-Theorem, a fundamental principle in Hilbert-Ackerman style formal systems. In the realm of philosophy and epistemology, we explore the logical equivalence between truth and satisfaction as established by Tarski, and the truth definition it produced. We also examine the concept of analyticity as defined by Carnap, along with alternatives proposed by Godel and Rosser, and other perspectives on the problem of induction raised by Goodstein.

This article examines the instability of invariant subsets in dynamical systems with fractional-order by using an illustrative example. A fractional-order linear system is used to demonstrate how even minor deviations from an initial condition can result in significantly divergent behavior, highlighting the importance of invariant manifolds in assessing system stability.

This study presents a novel structural acoustic inverse problem where the objective is to determine the vibration shape of a screen located on an airfoil, given the modified acoustic spectrum of the surrounding flow. To tackle this complex task, deep neural networks were trained to map acoustic spectrum data to vibration patterns. A sophisticated optimization technique was used to verify the obtained solutions. The effectiveness of the proposed method was confirmed through a set of simulated experiments.

Within the simplest variant of the "scoto-seesaw" model, our analysis confirms that a democratic secouler mechanism is feasible among neutrinos and neutral fermions that lack mass initially. By incorporating radiative mass generation for neutral fermions, we've optimized parameter spaces and integrated various physical theories including electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino oscillation patterns, Higgs boson interactions, vacuum stability conditions, and production mechanisms at particle colliders. Through meticulous examination of data from colliders and neutrino oscillation experiments, we've derived constraints on secular mixing angles and generated predictions for potential new physics phenomena. Moreover, we've established parameter ranges that accommodate neutrino oscillation patterns and contribute to mass oscillation patterns while satisfying conditions for electroweak symmetry breaking. Notably, we've identified a viable solution where all neutrino oscillation patterns can be explained within the model without conflicting with existing physics frameworks. Additionally, our analysis has yielded constraints on coupling constants and mixing angles through various sources of physics including tree-level Higgs potential terms, dark sector mixing, dark sector mass generation, and dark sector interactions. By leveraging these constraints, we've optimized parameter spaces and integrated various theories including dark sector models, "next-to-minimal" supersymmetric extensions, and $U(1)$ extensions without charge parity symmetry. Within the secouler framework, we've computed mixing angles between Higgs bosons and neutral fermions as well as angle of ownership between dark neutral fermions and mass
